title: Russia: African leaders must use summit to call for an end to trafficking of Africans into Russian military
content:
African leaders attending the Russia-Africa summit must call on the Russian authorities to immediately end the coercive and deceptive recruitment of African nationals into Russia’s military forces to fight against Ukraine, Amnesty International’s African section directors said in an open letter ahead of the summit, which takes place from 28 to 29 October in Moscow.

“For African leaders to remain silent on this issue would be a profound disservice to the people of their countries. We urge them to address this issue directly with the Russian authorities at the Russia-Africa Summit 2026 and call on Russia to take immediate steps to end these practices, which in many cases amount to trafficking — a crime under international law,” said directors of Amnesty International’s sections across Africa.

“At a moment when many African governments are speaking up about the enduring legacy of colonialism, and the importance of sovereignty and African agency in international affairs, they must reject any practice that treats nationals of African countries as a commodity for other countries’ political and military objectives.”

title: Sri Lanka: Outrageous organized crime bill granting authorities unchecked powers must be withdrawn
content:
A new bill before Sri Lanka’s parliament that grants the authorities sweeping arbitrary powers to tackle ‘organized crime’ and deny suspects’ human rights should be immediately withdrawn, Amnesty International said today. 

The Prevention of Organised Crimes bill, tabled in Sri Lanka’s parliament on 6 October, contains provisions that would make confessions extracted under duress admissible in court, enable the detention of suspects for up to two years without trial, and ban the media from reporting on court proceedings. The bill also confers the police with wide powers to conduct searches without a warrant, and imprison people for not providing information to authorities.  

The bill mirrors many elements of Sri Lanka’s repressive Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), which has been misused since the 1970s to target minorities and repress dissent. 

“This extraordinary bill is the most alarming in a string of repressive laws proposed by the National People’s Power (NPP) government. It reintroduces most of the very worst elements of the PTA and applies them to a wide range of offences,” said Smriti Singh, Amnesty International’s South Asia Director.

title: Egypt: Court order to shut down and fine Mada Masr a devastating blow to media freedom
content:
Responding to the news that the New Cairo Misdemeanours court today convicted editor in chief Lina Attalah on charges of operating an unlicenced website, ordering the shutdown of prominent independent outlet Mada Masr and taking her into police custody pending payment of the maximum penalty of three million EGP fine (54,467 USD) Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Regional Impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said: 

Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.

Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International

Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.

“Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country. By imposing a 3 million EGP fine, ordering the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its property, and detaining Lina Atallah until payment is made, the Egyptian authorities are sending a clear and ruthless message: critical, independent reporting will not be tolerated.

title: CAR: Special Criminal Court, the last hope of justice for thousands, on the brink of collapse – new report
content:
• Special Criminal Court at risk of closure by 2028 with thousands of victims awaiting justice
  • Other than the UN and the EU, no state providing financial support to SCC at the moment
  • ICC closed investigations; National courts lack resources and independence to take on SCC cases

    • Suspected perpetrators of crimes under international law in the Central African Republic (CAR), including some of the country’s highest-ranking officials, are at risk of escaping justice unless the Special Criminal Court (SCC) receives the funding it requires to continue investigating and prosecuting cases, Amnesty International said in a new report.

title: France: Lawmakers must reject regressive “Rioters Pay” bill
content:
France’s proposed bill to make demonstrators pay for damage caused to property by acts of violence in street protests, even if they did not directly cause it themselves, will have a chilling effect on freedom of peaceful assembly and must be rejected by lawmakers, Amnesty International said ahead of a two-day debate in the Senate. 

This bill threatens to further deter people from exercising their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly 

Nathalie Godard, Amnesty International France

This bill threatens to further deter people from exercising their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly 

If passed, the legislation commonly referred to as the “Rioters Pay” bill, could hold individuals liable for acts they did not personally commit, provided they ‘knowingly’ participated in a gathering where acts of violence, theft, destruction, or property damage took place. A protester could be liable to pay up to 10,000 euros; in addition, social benefits could be seized if compensation is not paid, which risks plunging already marginalised families further into poverty. Parents may also be held civilly liable for acts that their children did not commit.

title: Russia: Exiled advocate faces “extremism” charges over human rights work for Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO Memorial
content:
Reacting to news that a prosecutor’s office in Moscow is about to initiate criminal proceedings on “extremism” charges against prisoners’ rights advocate Anna Karetnikova, from the Memorial Human Rights Centre, who is currently living in exile, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:

“Amnesty International has long warned of the danger that Russia’s vague and overly broad anti-extremism legislation would be used to criminalize lawful human rights work. Today, those fears are being realized with the criminal case against Anna Karetnikova – the first time such charges have been used against an individual solely because of their human rights work.”

“Although Anna Karetnikova is living in exile and can only be tried in absentia, the threat of prosecution sends a chilling message that is intended to silence human defenders in Russia and abroad, stop them from documenting violations and deter them from speaking up for the victims of these abuses. Criminalizing the human rights work of a leading, Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO is a harmful and shameful move that further exposes Russian authorities’ true motives.

title: I am targeted by the military because I work for Amnesty, but I refuse to let fear win
content:
Usman Hamid, the Executive Director of Amnesty International Indonesia, has spent decades as a human rights defender. But the relentless campaigns of harassment and intimidation designed to silence him have a new dimension in the digital age.

My journey into human rights activism was forged in the blood that stained the pavement of Trisakti University. In my teenage years, my mother got me involved in organizing assistance for people living in poverty. I began to witness the stark socio-economic disparities that existed under former president Suharto, amid widespread corruption and state repression. By May 1998, public frustration had reached boiling point, sparking student protests across Indonesia. What began as a growing unease with social injustice drew me into the movement. But it was the killing of four of my classmates at Trisakti on 12 May 1998 that transformed my concerns into a lifelong commitment to human rights activism.

title: Israel/OPT: Elections must not deflect attention from Israel’s international crimes
content:
Ahead of parliamentary elections in Israel on 27 October, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Research, Policy, Advocacy and Campaigns said:

“While much of the world’s attention is focused on Israel’s upcoming parliamentary elections, Palestinians who have endured decades of crimes and systematic violations at the hands of successive Israeli governments have little reason to expect the outcome to deliver positive human rights change.  

“In recent months, electoral candidates have shamelessly exploited anti-Palestinian sentiment or even threatened to step up human rights violations and crimes under international law in a bid to score political points. Candidates have used dehumanizing rhetoric against Palestinians, promised to further entrench Israel’s illegal annexation measures in the occupied West Bank, and threatened further devastation of the occupied Gaza Strip. Candidates across the political spectrum also pushed for the disqualification of Sami Abu Shehadeh, Palestinian citizen of Israel and chairperson of the Tajammou’ (Balad) party, displaying utter disregard for the right to freedom of association, expression, and assembly.

title: Cuba: Two years after being named prisoners of conscience, Félix Navarro, Sayli Navarro and Roberto Pérez Fonseca must be released
content:
On 23 October 2024, Amnesty International named Félix Navarro, Sayli Navarro and Roberto Pérez Fonseca prisoners of conscience, concluding that they had been deprived of their liberty solely for peacefully exercising their human rights. Two years later, they remain unjustly imprisoned amid the continued politically motivated detention and repression of critical voices in Cuba.

In response, Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director, said:

“Two years after being named prisoners of conscience, Félix Navarro, Sayli Navarro and Roberto Pérez Fonseca remain unjustly deprived of their liberty. That means two more years separated from their families, subjected to the harsh conditions of Cuba’s prison system and punished solely for exercising their human rights. The Cuban authorities must release them immediately and unconditionally. They should not spend another day behind bars.”

title: Sudan: El Fasher civilians suffer unlawful killings, detention and torture one year after city’s capture by the RSF – new testimony
content:
• Surveillance and detentions rife in city
  • With limited humanitarian aid, risks of child malnutrition remain high
  • “A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today” – Agnès Callamard

    • Civilians in El Fasher in North Darfur, Sudan, are still suffering detention, torture and limited access to humanitarian aid one year after the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured the city and committed brutalities against civilians, Amnesty International said today.

    In new testimony, residents who recently escaped the city told Amnesty International how schools had been turned into detention centres, how their movement was strictly controlled, and that unlawful killings were rife.

    According to figures gathered by humanitarian organizations working in the city, fewer than 70,000 people are present in El Fasher, compared to its pre-war population of more than one million. Humanitarian access remains limited, and humanitarian workers and other civilians in the city are constantly surveilled or monitored. Arbitrary detention risks, for both civilians and humanitarian workers, remain extremely high.

    A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today

    Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General

title: Convention on Biological Diversity. What you need to know and why it matters
content:
You have probably heard of the UN Convention on Climate Change, which emerged from the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. What is less well known is that two further conventions were also born at the summit: the Convention to Combat Desertification, and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). The three were always intended to be implemented together as humankind’s response to the global environmental crisis. The aims of the CBD, which has been ratified by almost every country on the planet, are the conservation of nature, the sustainable use of its products (for example timber from rainforests) and the sharing of benefits fairly by everyone.  

Every two years, states that have joined the CBD meet in a “Conference of the Parties” (COP), the global decision-making body that oversees implementation of the convention. This year’s meeting is the 17th – known as COP17. In 2022, in response to challenges including massive-scale deforestation and extinction-level declines in the populations of many species, CBD’s COP15 agreed the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework which sets out 23 targets for nature conservation.

title: Yemen: Huthis must open Ta’iz roads immediately as thousands of civilians’ lives are at risk
content:
The Huthi de facto authorities must immediately open vital roads in and around Ta’iz city, as fighting intensifies between the Huthis and government forces and moves closer to densely populated areas of the city, Amnesty International said today.  

The Huthis have tightened their control around Ta’iz city after they cut off the main road connecting Ta’iz to Aden in October, pushing the city to the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster. They have blocked humanitarian aid, putting access to food, water, and healthcare for hundreds of thousands at grave risk as per UN agencies. 

“The residents of Ta’iz, Yemen’s third largest city, have endured years of hardship due to the conflict, while hosting the country’s largest number of internally displaced people. At various points since 2015, Huthi forces have surrounded the city, blocking access to major roads connecting it  to other towns and cities and forcing civilians to use dangerous and poorly maintained mountained roads,” said Heba Morayef, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for Middle East and North Africa.

title: EU: Frontex reform compounds risk of EU complicity in rights violations
content:
Responding to the European Commission’s proposed reform of the European Border and Coast Guard Regulation (the Frontex Regulation) that vastly expands the agency’s budget, powers, staff and mandate, without commensurately expanding its human rights safeguards and transparency obligations, Eve Geddie the Director of Amnesty International’s European Institutions Office said:

“The European Commission’s proposed changes to the Frontex mandate once again prioritize expanding the agency’s powers to deport, enforce border control, and operate beyond the EU without expanding the agency’s human rights obligations in turn.

“This includes giving Frontex new powers to carry out forced returns between non-EU countries, paving the way for a broader role in ‘return hubs’ in third countries. This reform compounds the risk of EU complicity in human rights violations and raises further hurdles to transparency and accountability. It should be rejected outright.

title: Tanzania: Authorities weaponize counterterrorism laws to restrict civic space amid pervasive impunity over violent election crackdown
content:
Tanzanian authorities have failed to hold anyone accountable for the violence security forces inflicted on protesters, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured in the wake of the 2025 general election, Amnesty International said on the first anniversary of the crackdown.

Instead of delivering justice and accountability, authorities have withheld a Commission of Inquiry report from the public and intensified attacks on civic space through the abuse of counterterrorism laws.

Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters. In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponizing counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear,”

Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
